summary: Describes a protocol for posting messages from workstations, such as PCs, to a mail service host. It is an Experimental protocol that handles sending, not retrieving, mail.

eli5.summary: It is a way for a small computer to hand its outgoing mail to a bigger mail computer for delivery.

questions: what is the message posting protocol
how do pcs authenticate with mail servers
subtitle: Protocol for personal computers to submit outgoing mail to a mail service host.

tldr.problem: Personal computers lack operating-system-level user authentication mechanisms, which is essential for email systems to prevent mail forgery and ensure senders' identities are verified.
tldr.mechanism: MPP defines a simple command-reply protocol over TCP that allows a PC to authenticate with a mail server using username and password, then submit messages for delivery to the wider email system.
tldr.outcome: The protocol enables PCs to integrate into email networks by handling authentication at the server level before submission to mail delivery systems like Sendmail or MMDF.

today: RFC 1204 is an Experimental protocol from 1991. It was never widely adopted, as later developments in email authentication (including POP3 with authentication and SMTP authentication extensions) provided standardized solutions for remote message submission.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
Personal computers running operating systems like MS-DOS do not provide operating-system-level user authentication. This creates a problem for email: the email system must authenticate a sender's identity to prevent mail forgery. The solution is to use an intermediary agent called a message posting server that authenticates the sender and then submits mail to the message delivery system on behalf of the sender.

The Netix Message Posting Protocol defines the interface between the message posting server (running on a trusted host) and the PC client. The protocol uses TCP and is based on command-reply structures from RFC 821 (SMTP) and RFC 959 (FTP).
sections.eli5: Your computer at home does not have a secure way to prove who you are. So you log in to a trusted mail server, and it sends your mail for you.

sections.title: Commands and Reply Codes
sections.content:
The protocol defines five main commands. USER informs the server of the username attempting to send mail, restricted to three conditions: session start, after successful message submission, or after a syntax error on a previous USER command. PASS provides the password associated with the previously specified username.

DATA instructs the server to accept mail message text, followed by the client sending lines of message content terminated by a bare period on its own line (matching RFC 821 convention). NOOP tests the status of the server without performing any action. QUIT terminates the session.

Reply codes follow SMTP conventions: 220 (service ready), 250 (command OK), 354 (ready for message), 451 (local error), 500 (unrecognized command), 501 (syntax error), 503 (illegal command sequence), 530 (authentication failure), and 550 (error).
sections.eli5: The protocol has simple commands: tell your name, give your password, say you want to send a message, send the message, and hang up.

sections.title: Server Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several implementation issues for message posting servers. Security is paramount: the server must run in a secured environment with restricted physical and network access. Port 218 is assigned for the protocol.

Idle client handling should terminate sessions if no activity occurs for too long to free resources. For username and password verification, servers can leverage existing password databases (such as UNIX passwd files) using FTP and POP3, or maintain a local password file specified by the system administrator. The server should accept any syntactically correct username and return 250 to avoid leaking information about which usernames exist.

Accepted messages should be queued and submitted to the message delivery system immediately. Message delivery failures should be handled by the message delivery system itself, not by the message posting server.
sections.eli5: The server needs to be careful about security, not keep clients connected forever, and pass messages to the real mail system quickly.

sections.title: Security and Operational Status
sections.content:
The MPP protocol addresses one specific security problem: authenticating the originator of a message before it enters the mail system. By requiring username and password authentication on the message posting server, the server can verify that a PC user is who they claim to be before accepting their mail.

RFC 1204 remains an Experimental specification rather than a standard. While it provided an early approach to the problem of mail authentication from untrusted clients, later solutions like SMTP authentication extensions (SMTP AUTH) became the standardized approach for client authentication in the Internet email ecosystem.
sections.eli5: The main security idea is to check who you are before letting you send mail. Later standards provided better ways to do this.
